372.title: Ashvala asks about death and ritual (3.1)
372.hook: the king's own hotri priest asks how a ritual can free anyone from death, and Yajnavalkya answers by turning each priest into a part of you
372.tomorrow: Artabhaga: "when a man dies, what does not leave him?"
372.howItsDone: Vedic fire rituals, with their four kinds of priests, are still performed in parts of India; Hindu homes and temples keep smaller fire offerings, and Vedanta teachers read passages like this as showing the inner meaning of the rite.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a thousand cows with gold on their horns, and Yajnavalkya's answer: we bow to the wisest, we just want the cows. Your line was who is the wisest? Did you answer something without proving yourself first? Day three hundred seventy-two.

The first challenger is a professional. Ashvala is King Janaka's hotri, the priest whose job at the great fire sacrifice is to recite the hymns of the Rig Veda. He has spent his life inside the ritual: the right verse, the right moment, the right pitch. So he doesn't ask about the meaning of life. He asks about his own job. You think you're the wisest? Fine. Explain to me how what I do actually works.
screen: `THE FIRST CHALLENGER.` → `A PROFESSIONAL PRIEST.` → `EXPLAIN MY OWN JOB TO ME.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, Ashvala says, everything here is caught by death. By what does the one who offers the sacrifice get free of death? By the hotri priest, Yajnavalkya answers, by fire, by speech. Speech is the hotri of the sacrifice. Speech is this fire. And that is freedom. That is freedom beyond. Ashvala tries again. Everything is caught by day and night. How does one get free of them? By the priest who handles the offerings, by the eye, by the sun. Everything is caught by the waxing and waning moon. By the priest who sings, by breath, by wind. And the sky has no stairs. How does the sacrificer climb to heaven? By the priest who oversees, by the mind, by the moon. Notice the pattern. Each of the four priests of the great sacrifice turns out to be a part of the person, speech, eye, breath, mind, and each of those turns out to be a power of the cosmos, fire, sun, wind, moon. Yajnavalkya doesn't tell Ashvala the ritual is useless. He shows him what it's a picture of. The priest at the fire is also the voice in your throat. Then Ashvala asks a string of technical questions, how many verses, how many offerings, and Yajnavalkya answers each one. And Ashvala falls silent. Hindu thinkers have weighed this differently. The Mimamsa school held that the rites themselves are the heart of the Veda. Vedanta teachers read passages like this one as the rites pointing past themselves. Both kept the rites, and the fire rites are still performed today.
screen: `CAUGHT BY DEATH: HOW TO GET FREE?` · `THE PRIEST IS SPEECH; SPEECH IS FIRE.` · `FOUR PRIESTS, FOUR FACULTIES, FOUR POWERS.` · `ASHVALA FALLS SILENT.` · then, large: `FREEDOM, AND FREEDOM BEYOND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the four priests inside you. Sit, and breathe. First, notice speech, even unspoken: the words forming in your mind. Let it be the fire. Then the eyes, resting closed: let them be the sun. Then the breath, coming and going: the wind. Then the mind, watching all of it: the moon. Nothing to perform. You're the whole ritual, sitting still. The bell holds the time.
Atimukti, freedom beyond. Ashvala's answer: the freedom the rite points to, when the priest is understood as speech, and speech as fire.
Your line: the priest who goes beyond. Today, take one routine you do on autopilot and ask what it's a picture of. Day three hundred seventy-two.

373.title: Artabhaga: "when a man dies, what does not leave him?" — karma (3.2)
373.hook: asked what's left of a person after death, Yajnavalkya takes his questioner's hand and walks him out of the room
373.tomorrow: Bhujyu asks where the Parikshitas went
373.howItsDone: Hindus remember the dead by name in shraddha rites, offering food and water to ancestors named in a family line; teachers of the Upanishads point to Artabhaga's dialogue as an early statement of karma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, atimukti: Ashvala the priest asked how ritual frees anyone from death, and each priest turned out to be a part of the person. Your line was the priest who goes beyond. What routine turned out to be a picture of something? Day three hundred seventy-three.

The second challenger is Artabhaga, and his last question is one people still ask. When a person dies, he says, their speech goes into fire, their breath into the wind, their eye into the sun, their mind into the moon, their body into the earth, their hair into the plants and trees, their blood into the waters. Then where is that person? And this time, Yajnavalkya won't answer in front of the crowd. Artabhaga, my friend, he says. Take my hand. This is for the two of us alone.
screen: `EVERYTHING GOES BACK.` → `THEN WHERE IS THAT PERSON?` → `TAKE MY HAND.`

segments.voice: Artabhaga's questions start dry. How many graspers are there, and how many over-graspers? Eight, Yajnavalkya says. The tongue grasps, and taste grasps it back. The eye grasps, and form grabs the eye. The ear and sound, the mind and desire, the hands and work. Everything we take hold of takes hold of us. Then closer to the bone. When a person dies, do the breaths leave them? No, they gather inside; the body swells and lies still. Then: when a person dies, what does not leave them? The name, Yajnavalkya says. The name is endless. So far, all of it in public. Then the last question, where is the person when everything has gone back, and the hand, and the walk out of the room. The text tells us only this about their private talk. What they talked about was karma. What they praised was karma. A person becomes good by good action, and bad by bad action. And Artabhaga fell silent. Karma means action, the thing you do, and it had been a word of the ritual: the rite performed correctly. Here, two people step outside and talk about it as the thread of a person's life, carried past death. Some readers hear in it an early statement of the idea in the Upanishads. Why whisper it? The text doesn't say. Some think the teaching was new; some think it was simply too serious for a contest. Either way, a crowd waited outside while two men held hands and talked about what we do.
screen: `EVERYTHING WE GRASP GRASPS US.` · `WHAT DOES NOT LEAVE? THE NAME.` · `WHAT THEY PRAISED WAS KARMA.` · `GOOD BY GOOD ACTION, BAD BY BAD.` · then, large: `THE NAME.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a name. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who has died, someone you knew, or someone you've only heard of. Say their name silently. Notice that it still does something: it still brings a face, a voice, a way of doing things. Then let one of the things they did come to mind, one action, good or ordinary. Hold the name and the action together. The bell holds the time.
Artabhaga. The questioner Yajnavalkya took aside, and the word the two of them praised in private: karma, action, the thing you do.
Your line: the name. Today, say the name of someone who has died, out loud or to someone else, and mention one thing they did. Day three hundred seventy-three.

374.title: Bhujyu asks where the Parikshitas went (3.3)
374.hook: the third challenger brings a question he got from a spirit, and already knows the answer
374.tomorrow: Ushasta: "the self within all — show me"
374.howItsDone: Vayu, the wind, is honored in Hindu tradition as a deity and as the cosmic breath; in this Upanishad's debate, Yajnavalkya's answer to Bhujyu is read as praise of wind as both the individual and the whole.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Artabhaga asked what doesn't leave a person at death. The name. And then, privately, karma. Your line was the name. Did you say one name out loud? Day three hundred seventy-four.

The third challenger opens with a ghost story. When I was a student, says Bhujyu, we wandered to a house in the land of the Madras. The householder's daughter was possessed by a spirit, a gandharva. We asked it who it was, and it told us its name. Then we asked it about the ends of the world, and where the Parikshitas went. So, Yajnavalkya, I'm asking you. Where did the Parikshitas go? It's a trap with the answer already in his pocket. He heard it from a spirit. Let's see if this man knows it too.
screen: `A SPIRIT IN A STUDENT'S STORY.` → `IT KNEW THE ENDS OF THE WORLD.` → `WHERE DID THE PARIKSHITAS GO?`

segments.voice: Who were the Parikshitas? The family of King Parikshit, remembered as great performers of the horse sacrifice, the one that opened this Upanishad two weeks ago. The Mahabharata tells of a Parikshit too: Arjuna's grandson, born after the war. The Upanishad doesn't explain any of that; it assumes its listeners know. Yajnavalkya answers without a pause. The spirit told you, surely, they went where those who perform the horse sacrifice go. And where is that? Then he gives a map. This world is as wide as thirty-two days of the sun's chariot. The earth surrounds it, twice as wide. The ocean surrounds the earth, twice as wide again. And between them is a gap as thin as the edge of a razor, or the wing of a fly. Through that gap, Indra, taking the form of a bird, handed the Parikshitas to the wind. And the wind carried them to where the horse-sacrificers are. Then the key line: so wind is each single thing, and wind is everything together. Whoever knows this, the text says, escapes dying again. And Bhujyu falls silent. Notice what's being praised. Not a gate, not a bridge. The way out of the world is narrower than a razor, and what carries you through is wind, the great breath of the cosmos. Twelve days ago, breath was the one singer the demons couldn't pierce. Here, the same power, at the scale of the universe, is what carries a person beyond the world. It belongs to every single one of us, and to everything at once.
screen: `THE FAMILY OF KING PARIKSHIT.` · `THIRTY-TWO DAYS OF THE SUN'S CHARIOT.` · `A GAP THIN AS A RAZOR'S EDGE.` · `WIND: EACH THING, AND ALL TOGETHER.` · then, large: `BEYOND THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Two minutes at the razor's edge. Sit, and breathe. Notice the tiny gap at the top of each in-breath, before the out-breath begins. It's thin, thinner than a fly's wing. Don't hold it; just notice it each time. Then notice that the air moving through you is the same air moving through the trees outside, and the city, and the sea. Each breath yours; all breath shared. The bell holds the time.
Vayu, wind. Yajnavalkya's answer: through a gap as thin as a razor's edge, carried by vayu, each single thing and everything together.
Your line: beyond the world. Today, step outside once and feel the wind, or just the air, on your face, and remember it's the same air everywhere. Day three hundred seventy-four.

375.title: Ushasta: "the self within all — show me" — "you cannot see the seer of seeing" (3.4)
375.hook: a challenger some identify with a famine survivor from the Chandogya demands to be shown the self the way you'd point at a cow
375.tomorrow: Kahola: the self beyond hunger and thirst
375.howItsDone: Teachers of Advaita Vedanta use this passage in self-inquiry, inviting students to turn attention back toward the one who sees; commentators of several Vedanta schools discuss the line about the seer of seeing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhujyu's question from a spirit, and the razor-thin gap at the edge of everything. Vayu carried the Parikshitas through. Your line was beyond the world. Did you feel the air on your face? Day three hundred seventy-five.

The Chandogya, which we read last month, tells of a man named Ushasti Chakrayana, starving in a famine, who ate leftover beans from an elephant driver to stay alive. Then the driver offered him water, and he turned it down: water, he said, I can find anywhere. Some readers take him to be today's challenger, Ushasta Chakrayana. Whoever he is, he's practical. He doesn't want theory. He wants to be shown. Point to it, he says, the way you'd point to a cow.
screen: `A MAN WHO SURVIVED ON LEFTOVER BEANS.` → `NO THEORY.` → `POINT TO IT.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, he says, explain to me the Brahman that is right here, direct, not secondhand: the self that is within everything. That is your self, Yajnavalkya answers, within everything. Which one, Ushasta asks, is within everything? The one that breathes in with your in-breath and out with your out-breath. That is your self, within all. Ushasta isn't having it. You've explained it the way someone says, that's a cow, that's a horse. Pointing at a thing. I asked for the direct one. And here Yajnavalkya gives the answer this day is named for: na drishter drashtaram pashyeh. You cannot see the seer of seeing. You cannot hear the hearer of hearing. You cannot think the thinker of thinking. You cannot know the knower of knowing. That is your self, within all. Everything else is sorrow. And Ushasta falls silent. Here's why the cow won't work. Everything you can point to is something seen. The self isn't something seen. It's what's doing the seeing. Your eye sees the whole room and never once sees itself. A flashlight lights up the path, and the one thing it can't shine on is its own bulb. Yajnavalkya isn't dodging the question. He's saying Ushasta asked for it to be shown, and the one thing that can never be shown is the one looking. For Yajnavalkya, that doesn't make it far away. It makes it nearer than anything you could point to.
screen: `SHOW ME THE SELF WITHIN ALL.` · `NOT LIKE POINTING AT A COW.` · `YOU CANNOT SEE THE SEER OF SEEING.` · `THE EYE NEVER SEES ITSELF.` · then, large: `THE SEER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes looking for the looker. Sit, with your eyes open and soft. Notice what you see: a wall, a window, your hands. Now, gently, try to turn around and find the one who's seeing. You won't find it as a thing. Notice that. Close your eyes and do the same with sounds: hear, and then look for the hearer. Don't strain. Rest in not finding it, and in the seeing still going on. The bell holds the time.
Ushasta. The man who wanted the self pointed out like a cow, and heard about the drashta, the seer, who can never be seen, because it is the one looking.
Your line: the seer. Today, once, in the middle of looking at a screen, notice that something is seeing it. Day three hundred seventy-five.

376.title: Kahola: the self beyond hunger and thirst (3.5)
376.hook: the next challenger asks the very same question, word for word, and gets a completely different answer
376.tomorrow: Gargi, the woman who asked: on what is water woven?
376.howItsDone: Hindu renunciants, sannyasis, take vows giving up the desires for family, wealth and worlds that Yajnavalkya names here; Vedanta teachers speak of the six waves of hunger, thirst, grief, confusion, old age and death as what the self is beyond.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ushasta wanted the self pointed out like a cow, and heard: you cannot see the seer of seeing. Your line was the seer. Did you catch something seeing your screen? Day three hundred seventy-six.

Here's something odd about this debate. The next man to stand up, Kahola, asks exactly the same question Ushasta just asked. Word for word. Explain to me the Brahman that is right here, direct, the self within all. You'd expect Yajnavalkya to say: I just answered that. He doesn't. He answers again, and this time from a completely different side. Yesterday the self was the seer you can't see. Today it's what's left when hunger, grief and death have nothing to hold on to.
screen: `THE SAME QUESTION, WORD FOR WORD.` → `A DIFFERENT ANSWER.` → `WHAT'S LEFT?`

segments.voice: That is your self, within all, Yajnavalkya says. Which one? The one that is beyond hunger and thirst, beyond grief and confusion, beyond old age and death. Three pairs. Hunger and thirst belong to the body. Grief and confusion belong to the mind. Old age and death belong to a life. The self is beyond all three. Tradition calls these six the waves, the things that rise and fall on the surface while the depth stays still. Then Yajnavalkya says what knowing this does to people. Knowing this self, he says, the wise give up wanting sons, wanting wealth, wanting worlds, and live by begging. Wanting sons is really wanting wealth; wanting wealth is really wanting worlds. Both are just wanting. And then a surprising ladder. Having finished with learning, he says, one should want to live like a child. Having finished with being a child and with learning, one becomes a muni, a silent sage. Like a child. After all those years of memorizing the Veda, the next step isn't more knowledge. It's the plainness of a child. Readers hear that word, balya, in different ways. Some hear childlike simplicity: no showing off, no clever arguments. Shankara, the Advaita teacher, reads it as the strength that knowledge gives, playing on a Sanskrit word for strength. Either way, the scholars in this courtyard, who came to win cows with their learning, are being told that learning is a stage, not the summit. And Kahola falls silent.
screen: `BEYOND HUNGER, GRIEF AND DEATH.` · `WANTING SONS, WEALTH, WORLDS: JUST WANTING.` · `AFTER LEARNING, LIVE LIKE A CHILD.` · `THEN THE SILENT SAGE.` · then, large: `BEYOND.`

segments.voice: Two minutes like a child. Sit, and breathe. For now, set down everything you know: the Sanskrit words, the arguments, the names. Let them rest on the floor beside you. Look at the room the way a small child would, with no labels. Just shapes, light, sound. If hunger or a worry rises, let it rise, like a wave, and notice what it rises on. The bell holds the time.
Kahola. The one who asked Ushasta's question again, and heard about balya: childlikeness, the plainness that comes after learning, before the silence of the sage.
Your line: beyond. Today, when hunger, a worry or a deadline grabs you, say the word once to yourself, and notice what the wave is rising on. Day three hundred seventy-six.

377.title: Gargi, the woman who asked: on what is water woven? (3.6)
377.hook: a woman stands up in a courtyard full of men and asks a child's endless why, at the scale of the universe
377.tomorrow: Uddalaka: the thread and the inner controller
377.howItsDone: Hindu tradition remembers Gargi Vachaknavi as a philosopher of the Vedic age, and her questions to Yajnavalkya are studied as part of the Brihadaranyaka's great debate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kahola asked Ushasta's question again, and heard: beyond hunger, grief and death; after learning, live like a child. Your line was beyond. What wave did you watch rise? Day three hundred seventy-seven.

Why is it raining? Because of the clouds. Why are there clouds? Because of the water. Why is there water? A child can keep that chain going until the grown-up says, because I said so. Now put that chain in a royal courtyard, where a woman has just stood up among the learned men of the Kuru and Panchala lands. Her name is Gargi Vachaknavi. And she's about to ask Yajnavalkya why, again and again, all the way to the top.
screen: `WHY? AND WHY THAT?` → `A WOMAN STANDS UP.` → `ALL THE WAY TO THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Yajnavalkya, she says, everything here is woven, back and forth, on water. On what, then, is water woven? Weaving is her picture: threads running lengthwise and crosswise, each one held by another. On wind, Gargi, he says. On what is wind woven? On the worlds of the middle air. On what are those woven? On the worlds of the heavenly musicians. Then the worlds of the sun. Of the moon. Of the stars. Of the gods. Of Indra. Of Prajapati, the lord of creatures. And on what are the worlds of Prajapati woven? On the worlds of Brahman. On what, she asks, are the worlds of Brahman woven? And here he stops her. Gargi, don't ask too much, or your head will fall off. You are asking too far about a deity one shouldn't ask beyond. And Gargi falls silent. It's a startling moment. The same warning comes up more than once in this book, and here it marks the place where argument stops. Notice what kind of limit it is. Every answer so far named a thing, and you can always ask what holds a thing. But what holds everything isn't one more thread in the cloth. Asking what it's woven on is like asking what's north of the North Pole. Gargi isn't wrong to ask. She's found the edge of the question. And she isn't finished. In two days, she'll stand up again, and this time, she'll come armed.
screen: `ON WHAT IS WATER WOVEN?` · `WIND, AIR, SUN, MOON, STARS, GODS.` · `DON'T ASK TOO MUCH, GARGI.` · `THE EDGE OF THE QUESTION.` · then, large: `THE WEAVE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes asking Gargi's question. Sit, and feel what holds you. You on the seat. The seat on the floor. The floor on the building. The building on the earth. The earth held in space. Take a breath at each step. When you reach the last one you can name, don't push for another. Rest right there, at the edge, where the answers stop and you're still held. The bell holds the time.
Gargi. The woman who asked what everything is woven on, ota and prota, warp and weft, until the answers ran out at the edge of the question.
Your line: the weave. Today, when you touch a piece of cloth, a shirt or a towel, notice the threads, each one held by the others. Day three hundred seventy-seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: Gargi was silenced for asking too much.
what it means: she followed the chain of what holds what to its edge, where what holds everything isn't one more thread.
what a scholar hears: ota-prota, warp and weft (3.6.1); 'your head will fall off' is a warning heard more than once in the Brihadaranyaka's debates, and Gargi returns in 3.8.

378.title: Uddalaka: the thread and the inner controller (3.7)
378.hook: the salt-and-banyan father of the Chandogya steps up as a challenger, with a question a spirit once asked him
378.tomorrow: Gargi returns: "two questions, like two arrows"
378.howItsDone: The antaryamin passage is central in Sri Vaishnava theology, where God is understood as the inner ruler of all; students of other Vedanta schools study it too, and the antaryamin is invoked in devotional hymns.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gargi asked what everything is woven on, all the way to the top, until Yajnavalkya stopped her. Your line was the weave. Did you notice the threads holding each other? Day three hundred seventy-eight.

An old friend steps up. In the Chandogya, Uddalaka Aruni was the father who dropped salt in water and split a banyan seed for his son, and said: you are that. Now he stands up in Janaka's court as a challenger. And like Bhujyu, he brings a question from a spirit. Years ago, he says, a spirit speaking through a woman asked us: do you know the thread that strings this world, the next world and all beings together? Do you know the inner controller? Yajnavalkya, if you drive off those cows without knowing them, your head will fall off.
screen: `THE FATHER FROM THE CHANDOGYA.` → `A SPIRIT'S QUESTION.` → `THE THREAD, AND THE CONTROLLER.`

segments.voice: I know them, Yajnavalkya says. Anyone can say I know, I know, says Uddalaka. Tell us. The thread, says Yajnavalkya, is wind: like a string through beads, it holds this world and the next together. Then the inner controller, in a long chant. He who lives in the earth, yet is other than the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body the earth is, who rules the earth from within: he is your self, the inner controller, the deathless. Then again, the same lines, for water. For fire. For the sky, the wind, the sun, the directions, the moon and stars, space, darkness, light, all beings. Then it turns inward: the breath, speech, the eye, the ear, the mind, the skin, understanding. Over and over: he lives in it, it doesn't know him, it is his body, he rules it from within. And the close. He is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower. There is no other seer but him. And Uddalaka falls silent. Later schools built on this passage. Ramanuja, the Vishishtadvaita teacher, took its key phrase, whose body the earth is, and taught that the world and every soul are the body of God, who lives within them as their inner ruler. Shankara, the Advaita teacher, read the inner controller as the one self, appearing as ruler from the side of the world. Look back at this week of the debate. The priest. The name. The razor's edge. The seer. The child. The weave. And today, the one inside it all, unseen.
screen: `ANYONE CAN SAY I KNOW, I KNOW.` · `THE THREAD IS WIND.` · `WHOSE BODY THE EARTH IS.` · `THE UNSEEN SEER.` · then, large: `ANTARYAMIN.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the one within. Sit, and breathe. Feel the breath, and let the line come: lives in the breath, yet other than the breath. Then the eyes, resting: lives in the eye, yet other than the eye. Then the mind, with all its traffic: lives in the mind, yet the mind doesn't know it. You don't have to believe anything. Just notice whether something steady seems to sit under each of these, watching. The bell holds the time.
Uddalaka. The teacher who asked about the thread and the antaryamin, the inner controller: the one who lives in each thing, whom the thing doesn't know, and who rules it from within.
Your line: antaryamin. Today, touch the ground once, a floor or the earth, and remember: whose body the earth is. Day three hundred seventy-eight.

fork.setup: Uddalaka says: anyone can say I know, I know. you're Yajnavalkya. what do you do?
options: say exactly what the thread and the inner controller are.
fork.reveal: he tells them: the thread is wind; the inner controller lives in everything, unknown by it, ruling it from within. Uddalaka falls silent.

original.note: Sanskrit antaryāmin: antar (within) + yam (to hold, to rule): the one who rules from within.

trapdoor: what you thought: a controller, like someone pulling strings.
what it means: the one who lives in each thing, other than it, unknown by it, its inmost self.
what a scholar hears: the antaryāmi brāhmaṇa (3.7) is a key text for Ramanuja's śarīra-śarīri teaching, the world as God's body; Shankara reads it as the one self.
